desc:
The square grid describes an orchard. A cell holding -1 is a thorn bush that cannot be entered; any other cell holds that many gems (0 or more).

A collector starts in the top-left cell, walks to the bottom-right cell moving only right or down through cells that are not thorn bushes, and then walks back to the top-left cell moving only left or up through cells that are not thorn bushes. Whenever the collector stands on a cell it takes all gems there, and the cell is empty from then on (so gems of a cell are only counted once, even if both walks cross it).

Return the largest number of gems that can be collected on such a round trip. If there is no way to reach the bottom-right cell, return 0.
hints: The way back, read in reverse, is another right/down walk. So the task is to pick two right/down walks from corner to corner that together collect the most, counting a shared cell once.
Greedily taking the best first walk and then the best second walk is wrong, because the first walk can steal gems that the second walk needs. Move the two walkers simultaneously, one step each.

After t steps walker 1 is at (r1, t - r1) and walker 2 at (r2, t - r2), so the state is just (t, r1, r2). They stand on the same cell exactly when r1 == r2, and then the gems are counted once. Each walker came from above or from the left, giving four predecessor states.
editorial: Reverse the way back: the trip becomes two walks from the top-left to the bottom-right cell, both moving right or down, and the collected gems are the gems of the union of their cells. Optimising the two walks one after the other fails, because the first walk may take gems that make a worse first walk plus a better second walk the true optimum.

Advance both walkers together. After exactly t steps each walker has r + c = t, so the pair of positions is described by (r1, r2) alone. Let dp[t][r1][r2] be the most gems collected when the walkers are at those cells; two walkers on the same cell at the same time add its gems once, and since both walk monotonically they can never share a cell at different times. Transitions take the best of the four previous states (r1 or r1-1, r2 or r2-1) and add the gems of the cells (thorn bushes make the state invalid). The answer is dp[2n-2][n-1][n-1], or 0 if that state is unreachable. There are O(n) layers of O(n2) states, so the time is O(n3) and the space O(n2).
